props.title: The Concorde: Airport '79

sections.content: The Concorde: Airport '79 (1979) marks the desperate final gasp of the disaster film boom that dominated 1970s Hollywood. Following the massive success of Airport (1970), the franchise devolved into increasingly absurd scenarios, with this fourth entry featuring George Kennedy's recurring character Joe Patroni now inexplicably piloting the supersonic Concorde. The film epitomizes everything wrong with late 70s disaster films - wooden dialogue, improbable action sequences (including the Concorde doing aerial acrobatics to dodge missiles), and a cast of fading stars like Alain Delon and Susan Blakely trying to maintain dignity amid the chaos.

sections.content: The Airport series reflects the evolution of 1970s disaster cinema, from the relatively grounded original to increasingly outlandish sequels. Airport 1975 (1974) featured a small plane crashing into a Boeing 747, while Airport '77 (1977) somehow managed to sink a 747 in the Bermuda Triangle. By the time The Concorde: Airport '79 arrived, the genre had exhausted itself through repetition and escalating ridiculousness, paving the way for pitch-perfect parodies like Airplane! (1980). SUBHEAD: The Fall of Disaster Films

The failure of The Concorde effectively ended the golden age of disaster films that included classics like The Poseidon Adventure (1972) and The Towering Inferno (1974). These earlier films succeeded by combining spectacular practical effects with genuine human drama and all-star casts who took the material seriously. The genre wouldn't recover until the CGI era enabled new levels of destruction in films like Twister (1996) and Independence Day (1996), though these focused more on action spectacle than the ensemble drama approach of their 1970s predecessors.
